paras: The attempted lynching of Jack and Manuel Brown was an unsuccessful attempt, on the night of March 1, 1882, at Lexington, Mississippi, to lynch two young Black men charged with attacking the storekeeper A. H. Pinkston. The attempt failed, and the only report of it was a single sentence in a Mississippi weekly's column of state news.

According to the Lexington Advertiser, as quoted by the Brookhaven ledger on March 2, Pinkston was attacked and robbed in his store at Gary's Mill, in Holmes County, on the night of the 16th of the preceding month. The Advertiser called it "the most daring and atrocious assassination and robbery that ever occurred in Holmes county" and named Jack and Manuel Brown, "two colored youths" aged 16 and 18, as the perpetrators. Its wording does not say whether Pinkston survived.

On the night of March 1, at Lexington, "an unsuccessful attempt was made to lynch the two colored boys charged with attempting to murder A. H. Pinkston," in the words of the Panola weekly star of Sardis. The brief does not name the two boys, but the shared victim and charge suggest they were the Browns. It also gives no account of who made the attempt, where in Lexington it took place, or how it was stopped.
No report of an indictment, trial or later outcome for the two youths was found in the coverage.

Only white Mississippi papers carried the story, and they treated the crime and the mob differently. The Brookhaven ledger reprinted the Lexington Advertiser's description of the crime among its editorial items, presenting the youths' guilt as settled, but said nothing of a lynching attempt. The Panola weekly star mentioned the attempt in one unadorned sentence on March 11, set between an item on an escaped bigamist and a report of storm deaths, and used the more cautious "charged with." Neither paper commented on the mob.
The charge appears in two forms: the Advertiser spoke of an "assassination and robbery," while the Panola weekly star described the crime as an attempted murder, which implies that Pinkston lived.

bases: The Panola weekly star reported an unsuccessful attempt to lynch two Black youths held on a charge of attempted murder (A3); the attempt failed and no one was reported killed.
Only one report describes the lynching attempt (A3); the Brookhaven ledger (A1) confirms the underlying charge against two Black youths but says nothing of a mob.

framing.detail: The Panola weekly star gave the lynching attempt one unadorned sentence among miscellaneous state items, calling the accused 'colored boys'.

The Brookhaven ledger, quoting the Lexington Advertiser, called the crime 'the most daring and atrocious assassination and robbery that ever occurred in Holmes county' and named the youths as its perpetrators without qualification.

assassination and robbery perpetrated on the body of A. H. Pinkston

info: Night of the 1st inst. (March 1, 1882, in a March 11 paper)

Two 'colored boys' (A3), identified by the Lexington Advertiser as Jack and Manuel Brown, 'two colored youths' aged 16 and 18 (A1); that the two reports describe the same pair is inferred from the shared charge

Charged with attempting to murder A. H. Pinkston (A3); the Lexington Advertiser accused them of the assassination and robbery of Pinkston in his store at Gary's Mill on the night of the 16th ult. (A1)
